senses.gloss:
Vaikhānasa Āgama
(‘āgama belonging to the Vaikhānasa school’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Āgamas are secondary scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, more closely connected with rituals and temple culture. Of the three main branches of the āgamas—Śaivā-gamas, शाक्तागमस् and Vaiṣṇavāgamas—the last has split into two sampradāyas or traditions. They are: the पाञ्चरात्र आगमस् and the वैखानस आगम.
The latter derives its name from the sage विखनस् who was the founder.
Vikhanas, the Founder
Vikhanas was a sage of great anti-quity regarded as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु (or an emanation from him, of Vedic wisdom) who popularised the cult of विष्णु in the country. He is sometimes identified with the creator, the four faced ब्रह्मा, also. He is said to have written two treatises—the Vaikhānasa Kalpasūtras and the Daivikasūtras.
He had four chief disciples—Marīci, अत्रि, भृगु and Kāśyapa—to whom he taught the worship of विष्णु in great detail.
Iconographical works describe that he is white in complexion, is clothed in golden coloured garments and has four arms. He holds a दण्ड (staff) and has the ruru (antelope) as his mount. He is generally shown with his four disciples. His image has to be installed at the right side of the entrance to the मुखमण्डप (front porch) in a temple of विष्णु.
Vaikhānasa Literature
The original, basic, work was the Vaikhānasa Kalpasūtras which is not available now. A list of all the works composed by the four disciples may now be given:
By Atri (in 88,000 verses)
Ātreyatantra; Pūrvatantra; Uttaratantra; Viṣṇutantra.
By Bhṛgu (in 64,000 verses)
Arcādhikāra; Citrādhikāra; Khilādhikāra; Khilatantra; Kriyādhikāra; Mānādhikāra; Niruktādhikāra; Prakīrṇādhikāra; Pratigṛhyādhikāra; Purātantra; Varuṇādhikāra; Vāsādhikāra; Yajñādhikāra.
By Kāśyapa (64,000 verses)
Jñānakāṇḍa; Satyakāṇḍa; Tarkakāṇḍa.
By Marīci (1,84,000 verses)
Ānandasaṁhitā; Jayasaṁhitā; Jñānasaṁhitā; Saṁjñānasaṁhitā; Vijayasaṁhitā; Vijitasaṁhitā;Vimalasaṁhitā; Vīrasaṁhitā.
Only a few of these works have now survived. They are:
Ānandasaṁhitā and Jayasaṁhitā of मरीचि; Khilādhikāra, Kriyādhikāra, Prakīrṇādhikāra and Yajñādhikāra of भृगु; Jñānakāṇḍa of Kāśyapa; Uttara-tantra (or Samūrtārcanādhikāra) of अत्रि.
Some of the other, more important, works are:
Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa (of श्रीनिवास Makhin, A. D. 1050); commentaries on the Vaikhānasa Kalpasūtras and Sakalāgama-sārasaṅgraha by Nṛsīṁha-वाजपेय-Yājī; Lakṣmī-Viśiṣṭādvaita-bhāṣya on the Vedāntasūtrās of बादरायण, Uttama-brahmavidyā and Vaikhānasa mahima-mañjari by श्रीनिवास Makhin; Arca-nānavanīta by Keśavācārya; Prayogavṛtti (on the Vaikhānasasūtra) by Sundararāja; Vimānārcanakalpa by Raghunāthacakra-varti and Setumādhavācārya.
All the treatises of the वैखानस आगम series are distinguished by their meticulous attention to image-worship and temple rituals. They also give the essential aspects of temple architecture.
The Vaikhānasa Philosophy
Based on the commentary of श्रीनिवास Makhin on the Vedāntasūtras of बादरायण as mentioned above, one Raghupati Bhaṭṭācārya (also known as वासुदेव) composed a work called Mokṣo-pāyapradīpikā. Here he has systematised the philosophy of the Vaikhānasa आगमस् which is practically the same as the Viśiṣṭādvaita of Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137). It is in prose and has twelve sections.
Brahman or परमात्मन् is the highest and independent reality. He has two aspects: the niṣkala (devoid of form and attributes) and the sakala (with form and attributes).
In the sakala aspect he (known as विष्णु or नारायण) is inseparably associ-ated with लक्ष्मी, even as the मोओन् and its light are. He is ईश्वर, the supreme Lord, with the insentient प्रकृति (made up of the three guṇas सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्) and the sentient puruṣas (jīvas or individual souls)—which are also eternal—under his absolute control as dependent realities.
These jīvas who are atomic in size, are of three classes: नित्य (immutable or changeless like अनन्त [or आदिशेष], सनक and others); Mukta (emancipated, though once in bondage); and, baddha (bound, souls bound by their prārabdha-कर्म).
The baddha or the bound souls have been fettered, by being deluded by the māyā of ईश्वर (Viṣṇu) and can get लिबेरतिओन् only by seeking refuge in him, through devoted worship.
The means of लिबेरतिओन् are: ज्ञान (knowledge); upāsanā (worship); प्रपत्ति (surrender); कर्म (ritualistic action).
However, samārādhana (worshipping नारायण with intense devotion) is projected as the most effective sādhana. This can take any one of the following four forms: जप (repetition of divine name); huta or होम (fire-sacrifices); arcanā (iconic worship); ध्यान (meditation).
Whereas huta is the worship of God in the amūrta (an-iconic) form, arcanā in the iconic form has been declared to be the most effective of all.
Mukti (emancipation) is of four types: सालोक्य (to live in the world of God); सामीप्य (to live near God); sārūpya (to have a form similar to that of God) and सायुज्य (being united with or merged in God). The last is considered the real मुक्ति.
The Vaikhānasa treatises speak of four realms of विष्णु with one aspect of his, presiding over each. They are:
Āmoda Viṣṇu
Pramoda Mahāviṣṇu
Sammoda Sadāviṣṇu
Vaikuṇṭha Nārāyaṇa (or Vyāpi-नारायण)

The four types of मुक्ति mentioned are respectively related to these four realms. In the last state, the liberated सोउल् enters into the supreme light and enjoys everlasting bliss.
Corresponding to the four व्यूहस् of the Pāñcarātra system Vaikhānasa too posits four aspects of विष्णु who is called the आदिमूर्ति.
The four forms are: पुरुष, representing the quality धर्म (righteousness); सत्य, the quality ज्ञान (know-ledge); Acyuta, the quality ऐश्वर्य (glory); अनिरुद्ध, the quality वैराग्य (detachment).
Some aspects of योग like प्राणायाम, nāḍīs, कुण्डलिनी, and चक्रस् are also dealt with in the treatises of this Āgama.
The Vaikhānasa Community
The vaikhānasas are a community of temple priests. They are ordained by birth to be priests and have to follow only that avocation in life.
The sacramental rites that are prevalent in a vaikhānasa household include a unique ceremony called विष्णुबलि (or garbhacakrasaṁskāra). It is performed after the sīmanta (See SĪMANTONNAYANA for details), the ritual before childbirth conducted for the मोथेर्, in the bright half of the eighth month of pregnancy. It involves a होम and then offering to the pregnant मोथेर्, pāyasa (sweet rice-pudding) in which the emblem चक्र (discus-emblem of विष्णु) and शङ्ख (conch) have been previously dipped and a part offered in होम. While the woman is drinking it, a special मन्त्र is recited. The belief is that during this ritual, Lord विष्णु himself will brand the arms of the child to be born, with the marks of शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus), which he carries in his own hands.
The practical import of this ceremony is that the child born as a vaikhānasa has already been sanctified by विष्णु himself and hence needs no more initiatory rites as the Pāñcarātras do. He acquires the right to be a priest of विष्णु by birth. He can perform the worship both at home and in temples after formal training in the process of worship.
The vaikhānasas take to worship in temples as priests, not for eking out a living—such priests are called devalakas—but with a sense of duty and obligation. It is the responsibility of the temple management to provide for their maintenance.
The vaikhānasas bestow a very high place to the priest who worships in a temple. Whereas the icon acquires divinity after आवाहन (invoking), divinity, according to them, abides in him permanently.
Recitation of the Ātmasūkta (Vaikhā-nasa Saṁhitā, Mantrapraśna 5.49) enables the priest to get identified with the cosmic form of विष्णु.
Temple Images of Worship
The vaikhānasa mode of worship is essentially oriented towards विष्णु. In temples adopting this mode, there will generally be four or five icons of worship. The dhruvabera is the permanently fixed stone image. Next comes the कौतुकबेर, an exact replica of the original (but smaller in size) which receives the daily worship, hence being called arcanābera also. Then comes the snapanabera, an image used for naimittika or occasional rituals. Last is the utsavabera or autsavabera, used in worship for the sake of people who are motivated by worldly desires (kāmyārcanā).
The कौतुकबेर rests on an arcanā-पीठ, a seat of worship. The snapanabera is placed in another enclosure called snapanamaṇḍapa which is outside the sanctum. The utsavabera too has its own special place.
Viṣṇu is said to have taken three strides (vide Viṣṇusūkta 3). If the ध्रुव-बेर is विष्णु in the original posture, the three other images represent the same विष्णु in his three steps: कौतुकबेर is the first step, snapanabera, the second step and the utsavabera, the third step. It is the spirit of the same original icon that has entered into the other three.
Sometimes another icon is added to these three movable images, called the balibera. This is used for the sake of distributing ड़ोओद् daily to the attendant deities located in the enclosures.
If the same movable icon is used for all purposes, it is known as bhogabera.
Sometimes the system of having five icons for one deity is compared to the establishing of and maintaining the five Vedic fires (gārhapatya, आहवनीय, dakṣināgni, āvasthya and सभ्य).
Similar to the four व्यूहस् or emanations of the Pāñcarātra system, the Vaikhānasa system posits the चतुर्मूर्तिस्. विष्णु is the आदिमूर्ति. The four mūrtis or aspects are: पुरुष, सत्य, Acyuta and अनिरुद्ध.
They also correspond to the four icons in the temple: पुरुष is represented by the कौतुकबेर, सत्य by utsavabera, Acyuta by the snapanabera and अनिरुद्ध by the balibera. During the actual worship, however, अनिरुद्ध is omitted. The four images—kautaka, उत्सव, snapana and bali—are taken to represent विष्णु, पुरुष, सत्य and Acyuta respectively.
In the temple worship of the Vaikhā-nasa system, these four aspects of विष्णु are visualised as four forms located around him, in the immediate enclosure: पुरुष to the east; सत्य to the south; Acyuta to the west; and अनिरुद्ध to the north.
Iconographical works describe their images in different ways.
Conclusion
Though the Vaikhānasa आगमस् give primary importance to अर्चा or mūrtipūjā, to the images of gods, their consorts and attendant deities, the outlook is, in essence, idealistic. It holds that Godhead is sarvādhāra (support of all), sanātana (ancient and eternal), अप्रमेय (inscrutable), acintya (indefinable), nirguṇa (without attributes) and niṣkala (without parts). It is all-pervading even as butter in milk, oil in oil seeds or fire in firewood.
However, even as fire blazes forth by friction of the अरणि sticks, विष्णु appears in the heart of the devotee by ध्यान-mathana (churning due to meditation) or constant meditation. This is the ‘sakala’ form, the Absolute materialising itself due to the devotion and visualisation of the devotee.
Even then, worshipping an icon, properly prepared, and as per the rules given in the treatises, is extremely important. That itself can, ultimately, lead to salvation.
This seems to be the sine qua non of the Vaikhānasa आगमस्.
